question.problem:
Let $f(x)$ be the function defined below. For what value of $k$ is $f(x)$ continuous at $x=-1?$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{k}{x-1}, & x<-1 \\ 2x-k, & x\ge -1\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
From the definition of $f(x)$, the left-sided limit of $f(x)$ at $x=-1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -{1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -{1}^{-}}\frac{k}{x-1} \\  & =\frac{k}{-1-1} \\  & =-\frac{k}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -{1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -{1}^{+}}(2x-k) \\  & =2(-1)-k \\  & =-2-k.\end{aligned}
$$

We also note that $f(-1)=-2-k.$ 

So, for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=-1,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -{1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -{1}^{-}}f(x) \\ -2-k & =-\frac{k}{2} \\ -4-2k & =-k \\ k & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=-4$ removes the discontinuity at $x=-1.$
